1: At Jetavana, Venerable Dabba Mallaputta served as the Saṅgha’s steward, handing out meal tickets to the monks each morning.
2:
On days he got poor food, Venerable Lāludāyī threw the ticket hall into disorder:
“Does only Dabba know how to give out tickets, and not we?”
3:
As he kept throwing the hall into disorder, the monks said, “Then do it yourself,” and handed him the ticket basket.
From then on Lāludāyī was the steward.
4: But he could not tell good rice from poor, nor did he know the order of seniority among the monks.
5:
He scratched marks on the wall and ground to show where each group stood; though the numbers changed the next day
and the marks no longer fitted, he gave out tickets by them.
6:
The monks said, “Marks fall too high or too low; the good rice goes by years since ordination,”
but he would not listen: “I trust only my own marks.”
7:
Because the monks were losing their share, the young monks and novices pushed him out as unfit,
and there was a great uproar.
8:
The Buddha said, “Lāludāyī causes others loss through his own foolishness, not only now but in the past too,”
and at Ānanda’s request he told a story of the past.
9: Long ago in Bārāṇasī the Bodhisatta was the king’s valuer. He priced elephants, horses and jewels fairly and paid their owners.
10: The greedy king thought, “This man will soon empty my treasury.”
11:
From his window the king saw a foolish, greedy countryman crossing the courtyard
and, thinking, “This man can do my valuing,” called him in.
12: To protect his wealth, the king made that man his new valuer.
13: He set prices as he pleased, without regard to true worth, yet because of his office his word was final.
14: Then a horse-dealer came from the north with five hundred horses.
15:
The foolish valuer priced all five hundred horses at a single measure of rice;
the king had the dealer given one measure of rice and put the horses in the stable.
16:
The dealer told his story to the Bodhisatta, the former valuer, who advised him to bribe the fool
and have him state the value of a measure of rice before the king.
17: The dealer bribed the foolish valuer and asked him to do so.
18:
Before the king, the dealer said,
“I accept the price of the horses, but please ask what a measure of rice is worth.”
19:
The king asked, “What are the five hundred horses worth?” “A measure of rice.” “And the measure of rice?”
Having taken the bribe, the fool said, “All of Bārāṇasī, inside and outside the walls.”
20:
The ministers, who had thought the land and kingdom priceless, clapped and laughed:
“So this great kingdom, king and all, is worth a measure of rice! What wisdom our valuer has!”
21:
The ministers mocked the king in a verse:
“What is a measure of rice worth? All of Bārāṇasī, inside and out, is worth one measure of rice!”
22: Shamed by their mockery, the king drove out the foolish valuer and gave the office back to the Bodhisatta.
23: “The foolish valuer then was Lāludāyī, and the wise valuer was I myself.”
